extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers and anyone interested in Hollywood labor disputes and the 2023 WGA strike
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic summary and timeline of the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike, covering causes, demands, negotiation timeline, strike rules, affected productions, responses, and the eventual agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of the strike
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase funding and job security for writers; Increase the size of writers' rooms; Limit the use of artificial intelligence in the writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these as the WGA's stated goals. After the tentative agreement the WGA secured increases to minimum wage, final compensation, pension and health fund rates, improvements to terms related to length of employment and size of writing teams, and increases to residual payments for domestic and foreign streaming works; and regulation of AI (see AI entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residuals from streaming media
rubrics_metrics.description: Residuals from streaming media were a primary point of disagreement; the WGA claimed that the AMPTP's share of such residuals had cut much of the writers' average incomes compared to a decade prior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains the structural difference between broadcast and streaming pay (MBA applied to broadcast but not streaming), gives the WGA estimate that its proposals would yield about US$429 million per year whereas the AMPTP's offer would yield $86 million, and notes WGA demands for success-based or increased residual payments for streaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on generative artificial intelligence (genAI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers demanded strict limits on generative artificial intelligence, and that the Agreement state that genAI would not be used to replace writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the WGA was willing to concede writers' own uses of tech but insisted on contractual language preventing studios from using genAI to replace writers. The ratified contract included AI regulation prohibiting exploitation of writers' material to train AI models, produce digital recreations, and efforts to use AI to reduce writers or their pay. The AMPTP presented proposals suggesting rules for AI content during negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory staffing and duration of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild proposals sought 'mandatory staffing' and 'duration of employment' terms to require all shows to be staffed with a minimum number of writers for a minimum amount of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AMPTP described these demands as a 'primary sticking point' and criticized them as requiring staffing 'whether needed or not.' The article frames this as a key contested contractual term in negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pension and health fund allocation per writer
rubrics_metrics.description: WGA proposed that each member of a writing team receives their own pension and their own health care funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AMPTP rejected the proposal and did not offer a counterproposal; however, the article reports a tentative agreement to shift 0.5% of negotiated minimums into pensions and health funds, and the final deal improved pension and health fund rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: WGA strike rules for members (prohibited activities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers were instructed that 'writers cannot do any writing, revising, pitching, or discussing future projects with companies that are members of the AMPTP.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guild also stated fiction podcasts produced by companies against which the Guild and its members are striking must stop production. The Guild noted it cannot punish non-Guild writers who work for companies under strike but may bar such writers from future Guild membership; the rules governed picketing and other conduct during the strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and application of the Minimum Basic Agreement (MBA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MBA established minimum wages for television and film writers but in television applied only to broadcast television and not to streaming television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses this distinction to explain why writers on streaming shows were paid less than broadcast counterparts doing similar work, and notes the MBA expired on May 1, 2023—context important to negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized methods of industrial action
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike action, work stoppage, and picketing were the methods used by the WGA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents picket locations, instructed picketing schedules (e.g., beginning May 2 at 1:00 p.m. PDT), and related union-organized activities; it also notes temporary cancellations of picketing for safety (e.g., poor air quality, Hurricane Hilary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Studios' operational and contractual responses (force majeure and showrunner duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios in some cases halted productions, reduced staff, or invoked force majeure clauses to terminate agreements; some studios told showrunners/producers to perform non-writer duties during the strike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples: use of force majeure by studios to terminate production agreements, and an ABC letter stating producers expected to perform 'a through h' services (e.g., cutting for time, small dialogue changes). This reflects a contested interpretation of permitted activity during the strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of negotiation positions via estimated financial impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiating positions were framed quantitatively (WGA estimated its proposals would yield US$429 million/year to writers while AMPTP's offer would yield about $86 million/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites these figures to illustrate the scale of disagreement and to contextualize the bargaining demands and offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desired protections for writers affected by industry changes (e.g., 'Peak TV', COVID aftermath)
rubrics_metrics.description: WGA framed demands as responses to industry structural changes—declines in residuals, workforce reductions and cancellations following COVID-19, and the effects of 'Peak TV'—seeking protections like guaranteed employment duration and staffing minima.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article links these industry phenomena to writers' bargaining positions and rationale for the demands listed above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome criteria recorded in the tentative and ratified agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The tentative agreement (and subsequent ratification) secured increases to minimum wage, final compensation, pension and health fund rates, improvements to employment length and writing team size, increases to residual payments for domestic and foreign streaming works, and AI regulation prohibiting exploitation of writers' material for AI training or digital recreations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry records the concrete contractual changes the WGA considered a successful outcome; the article notes the membership ratified the contract with 99% in favor.
